Jeff Hubbard spoke to reporters Thursday ahead of the funeral, struggling to find words to describe how much his youngest son meant to him and his family. Wonderful young man." Tragically, the Hubbards have gone through this anguish before. In 2004 their son, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, was on patrol in Iraq with his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro -- also from Clovis -- when a roadside bomb exploded, killing both. Jeff Hubbard says there's no way for a parent to prepare for the agony a second time. "They're each absolutely individual terrible instances that you deal with the best you can as you go forward," he said. Six months after Jared was killed, Nathan and Jason Hubbard decided to enlist and serve together -- to follow in their brother's footsteps. On August 22 after returning from a scouting mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, the Blackhawk helicopter carrying Nathan and 13 other soldiers crashed. Jason, who served in the same Army platoon, was in a separate helicopter when his brother went down and was ordered to secure the crash site. When he and his men reached the downed Blackhawk, Jason says he realized it was his brother's unit. "We also had to remove as many of the men as we could out of that helicopter," Jason remembered. "And I couldn't participate in that. I knew my -- I knew Nathan was in there. I tried several times to kind of gather myself, but I just -- I couldn't." Jason says as the men carried bodies out of the wreckage, he spotted his younger brother. "At one point they did carry Nathan by me. And that's when the reality, the complete reality, and complete understanding of the situation came to me and I began dealing with it." Under the Department of Defense sole survivor policy, Jason says he was told he will not be allowed to return to war. His wife and young son will join him at his base in Hawaii.  E-mail to a friend .

CLOVIS, California (CNN) — Jeff Hubbard fought back tears as he spoke about his son, a “great, great young man” who was killed last week in a helicopter crash in Iraq. It is the second time he has had to bury a son killed in the Iraq War.

Jeff and Peggy Hubbard with their sons: Army Spc. Jason Hubbard, left, and Cpl. Nathan Hubbard.

This time, the tragedy was made even more devastating. His third son, also a soldier in Iraq, was among the first to arrive at the scene of last week’s helicopter crash and watched as soldiers carried the remains of his brother, 21-year-old Army Cpl. Nathan Hubbard, from the wreckage.

Nathan’s flag-draped coffin arrived in Fresno earlier this week before being taken to his hometown of Clovis. Watch “We love you Nate” »

Hundreds of mourners gathered Friday to remember Nathan at St. Anthony of Padua, the same church where his oldest brother’s funeral was held in 2004. Nathan will be laid to rest at Clovis Cemetery, beside his brother, Jared.

Nathan and his other brother entered the military shortly after Jared was killed, in order to honor his sacrifice.

“Their decision to join the military was motivated by a love for their brother and a desire to serve their country,” the priest told mourners Friday. “The death of Jared touched him deeply. Losing a brother and a friend made a profound impact on him, and brought to his attention the seasons of war and grief and loss.”

Jeff Hubbard spoke to reporters Thursday ahead of the funeral, struggling to find words to describe how much his youngest son meant to him and his family.

“I want everybody to remember and celebrate Nate in their own way, the way they want,” he said. “We want him honored, remembered and celebrated — he was a great, great young man. Wonderful young man.”

Tragically, the Hubbards have endured this anguish before. In 2004, their son, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, was on patrol in Iraq with his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro — also from Clovis — when a roadside bomb exploded, killing them both.

Jeff Hubbard said there is no way for a parent to prepare for such agony a second time.

“They’re each absolutely individual terrible instances that you deal with the best you can as you go forward,” he said.

Six months after Jared was killed, Nathan and Jason Hubbard decided to enlist and serve together, following in their brother’s footsteps.

On August 22, after returning from a scouting mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, the Blackhawk helicopter carrying Nathan and 13 other soldiers crashed. Jason, who served in the same Army platoon, was in a separate helicopter when his brother’s aircraft went down and was ordered to secure the crash site.

When he and his men reached the downed Blackhawk, Jason said he realized it was his brother’s unit.

“We also had to remove as many of the men as we could out of that helicopter,” Jason recalled. “And I couldn’t participate in that. I knew my — I knew Nathan was in there. I tried several times to kind of gather myself, but I just — I couldn’t.”

Jason said that as the men carried bodies out of the wreckage, he spotted his younger brother.

“At one point they did carry Nathan by me. And that’s when the reality, the complete reality, and complete understanding of the situation came to me and I began dealing with it.”

Under the Department of Defense’s sole survivor policy, Jason said he was told he will not be allowed to return to war. His wife and young son will join him at his base in Hawaii.

Jeff and Peggy Hubbard are the parents of Army Spc. Jason Hubbard and Cpl. Nathan Hubbard. Nathan’s coffin, covered with an American flag, was brought to Fresno earlier this week before being taken to his hometown of Clovis.

On Friday, hundreds of people came together to honor Nathan at St. Anthony of Padua, the same church where funeral services were held in 2004 for his oldest brother. Nathan is to be buried at Clovis Cemetery next to his brother, Jared.

After Jared’s death, Nathan and another brother joined the armed forces as a way to honor him and his sacrifice.

“Their decision to join the military was motivated by a love for their brother and a desire to serve their country,” the priest said to those gathered Friday. “The death of Jared touched him deeply. Losing a brother and a friend made a profound impact on him, and brought to his attention the seasons of war and grief and loss.”

Speaking with reporters on Thursday before the funeral, Jeff Hubbard had difficulty putting into words what his youngest son meant to him and to the family.

“I want everybody to remember and celebrate Nate in their own way, the way they want,” he said. “We want him honored, remembered and celebrated -- he was a great, great young man. Wonderful young man.”

The Hubbard family had already endured a similar heartbreak. In 2004, their son, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, was patrolling in Iraq alongside his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro, who was also from Clovis, when a roadside bomb detonated and killed them both.

Jeff Hubbard said nothing can prepare a parent to face such suffering a second time.

“They’re each absolutely individual terrible instances that you deal with the best you can as you go forward,” he said.

Six months after Jared’s death, Nathan and Jason Hubbard chose to enlist together and serve side by side, following the path their brother had taken.

On August 22, after coming back from a scouting mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, the Blackhawk helicopter carrying Nathan and 13 other soldiers went down.

Jason, who was assigned to the same Army platoon, was flying in another helicopter when Nathan’s aircraft crashed. He was then ordered to help secure the crash scene.

When Jason and his soldiers arrived at the wrecked Blackhawk, he said he recognized that it belonged to his brother’s unit.

“We also had to remove as many of the men as we could out of that helicopter,” Jason recalled. “And I couldn’t participate in that. I knew my -- I knew Nathan was in there. I tried several times to kind of gather myself, but I just -- I couldn’t.”

As bodies were being carried from the wreckage, Jason said he saw his younger brother.

“At one point they did carry Nathan by me. And that’s when the reality, the complete reality, and complete understanding of the situation came to me and I began dealing with it.”

Because of the Department of Defense’s sole survivor policy, Jason said he was informed that he would not be sent back to combat. His wife and young son are expected to move with him to his base in Hawaii.

In Clovis, a community near Fresno, news of Nathan Hubbard’s death brought renewed heartbreak to neighbors, friends and veterans who had already mourned with the family once before. Local officials and residents described the Hubbards as a family known for service, sacrifice and a deep commitment to one another.

Nathan Hubbard had reportedly joined the Army after his brother Jared’s death, motivated in part by a desire to honor him. The brothers’ story became a stark reminder of the burden carried by military families during the Iraq war, particularly those with more than one child serving overseas.

The Pentagon said the helicopter crash was under investigation. Initial reports indicated the aircraft went down during a nighttime operation, and military officials said hostile fire was not immediately believed to be the cause.

For the Hubbard family, the official details offered little comfort. Their loss had become painfully familiar: two sons, both young, both sent to Iraq, both never returning home.

counterfactuals.output:
**CLOVIS, Calif. —** For the second time in less than two years, mourners filed into a church in this Central Valley city to stand beside the same grieving father, face the same folded flag and say goodbye to another son killed in Iraq.

Outside, a line of motorcycles, police cruisers and military vehicles stretched along the street. Inside, beneath the high ceiling and stained-glass windows, the casket of Army Sgt. Daniel Ramirez rested at the front of the sanctuary, draped in red, white and blue. His father, Miguel Ramirez, sat only a few feet away, his hands clasped tightly, his eyes fixed on the flag.

He had sat in nearly the same place before.

Ramirez’s older son, Marine Cpl. Luis Ramirez, was killed in Iraq during a roadside bombing 18 months earlier. Now Daniel, 24, was dead too, one of several soldiers killed when a military helicopter went down during a mission outside Baghdad. The crash left another Ramirez son, Army Spc. Adrian Ramirez, alive but shattered: he was serving nearby and was among the troops who reached the crash site in the chaos that followed.

Adrian did not know at first that his brother had been aboard.

“He saw the smoke,” said a family friend who spoke on behalf of the relatives. “He saw the wreckage. He saw what was left before anyone told him Daniel was gone.”

The funeral brought home, in the most intimate way, the cost of a war often measured in numbers but carried by families one name at a time. In Clovis, where the Ramirez boys had played baseball, attended local schools and grown up in a modest home decorated with family photographs and service flags, the deaths have become a sorrow shared across the community.

Miguel Ramirez, a quiet man who immigrated to the United States as a young adult and worked long hours in construction to raise his children, has now buried two sons who volunteered for military service after the Sept. 11 attacks.

“He never imagined he would have to do this once,” said Pastor Thomas Keller, who presided over the service. “No parent imagines that. To do it twice is a grief most of us cannot begin to understand.”

Daniel Ramirez was remembered by relatives as the family’s steady one — a younger brother who followed Luis into uniform but insisted he was making his own choice. He was described as disciplined, funny in private, fiercely protective of his siblings and deeply proud of serving with his unit.

His commanding officer, reading from prepared remarks, called Daniel “the kind of soldier others trusted without hesitation.”

“He carried his responsibilities with courage and humility,” the officer said. “He loved his family, he loved his country and he never failed the soldiers beside him.”

But the most difficult words came from Adrian, 22, who stood at the lectern in uniform, his voice breaking before he began. He had returned from Iraq only days earlier, escorting his brother’s body home.

He spoke briefly, pausing often.

“I didn’t get to save him,” Adrian said. “I didn’t even know it was him. I just knew somebody’s brother was in there. Then I found out it was mine.”

Several mourners lowered their heads. Miguel Ramirez covered his face.

Adrian said he and Daniel had crossed paths in Iraq only a handful of times, usually in hurried meetings on bases or over brief radio calls relayed through mutual friends. They joked about who would get home first, who would have to help their father fix the fence, who would buy dinner when all three brothers were finally back together.

Luis was already gone by then, and the family had placed his photograph on a living room shelf with his medals and the flag from his funeral. Daniel had promised his mother he would come home safely. Adrian had promised the same.

Only one of them did.

Military officials have said the helicopter crash remains under investigation. Early reports indicated the aircraft went down during a combat operation, though officials have not released a final cause. Insurgents in the area claimed responsibility, but U.S. officials have not confirmed whether hostile fire brought down the helicopter.

For the Ramirez family, the details of the crash offer little comfort. What remains are the fragments: a final phone call, a photograph in desert camouflage, the knock at the door, the arrival of uniformed officers, the long flight home.

Neighbors said the family’s home has been filled for days with relatives, veterans, church members and strangers bringing food, flowers and handwritten notes. American flags line the front yard. Two blue-star banners that once hung in the window have been replaced by gold.

At the cemetery, Daniel was buried near his brother.

A rifle detail fired three volleys. A bugler played taps. The flag was lifted from the casket, folded with slow precision and presented to Miguel Ramirez, who pressed it to his chest.

The officer kneeling before him spoke the familiar words — on behalf of a grateful nation — and for a moment the only sound was the wind moving through the trees.

Adrian stood behind his father, staring at the ground.

After the service, mourners lingered beside the graves. Some embraced the family. Others touched the casket before walking away. A few veterans saluted in silence.

Miguel Ramirez remained seated for several minutes, holding the folded flag from Daniel’s coffin. Then he looked toward Luis’s grave nearby.

Two sons, two wars within one war, two flags in one father’s arms.

“He gave this country everything a father can give,” Pastor Keller said later. “And somehow he is still standing.”

**A military family sent three sons to serve. Two came home under flags.**

*By Staff Writer*

The flag outside the Whitaker family’s small brick home has flown at half-staff twice.

Inside, on a hallway wall lined with school portraits, football photos and framed military certificates, two dress-uniform pictures now sit side by side: Army Sgt. Daniel Whitaker, 27, and Marine Cpl. Matthew Whitaker, 22 — brothers who were killed in Iraq less than two years apart.

Their father, Robert Whitaker, still pauses each morning beneath the photographs.

“You raise them to do what they believe is right,” he said, his voice catching. “But no father ever thinks he’ll have to bury one son, let alone two.”

The Whitakers were known in their community as a military family long before tragedy made them known for loss. Robert served in the Army in the 1980s. His wife, Elaine, volunteered with local veterans’ groups. Their three sons grew up hearing stories about service, sacrifice and duty — words that felt noble, Robert said, until they became unbearably personal.

Daniel, the eldest, enlisted first. Quiet and steady, he was the kind of big brother who fixed broken bikes, checked homework and made sure his younger siblings got home safely, his family said. He deployed to Iraq with an Army unit tasked with patrols and security operations.

He was killed when an explosive device struck his convoy outside Baghdad.

Matthew, the youngest, joined the Marines after Daniel’s death. Family members say he felt pulled toward service, even after seeing what war had already taken.

“We begged him to think about it,” Robert said. “And he told us, ‘Dad, Danny went because he believed in something. I have to live my life believing in something, too.’”

Matthew was killed during combat operations in Anbar province.

The news came in the same way both times: a knock at the door, uniformed officers on the porch, a mother collapsing before the words were finished.

“There’s a sound your house makes after that,” Robert said. “It’s quiet, but it’s not peace. It’s emptiness.”

Their surviving son, Andrew Whitaker, 25, also served in the military and returned home from Iraq. He says coming back when his brothers did not has left him with grief that is difficult to explain.

“People tell me I’m lucky,” Andrew said. “And I know I am. But luck feels heavy when your brothers are gone.”

Andrew keeps Daniel’s watch in a drawer beside his bed and Matthew’s dog tags hanging from the rearview mirror of his truck. He said the brothers were different in almost every way: Daniel reserved and protective, Matthew impulsive and quick to laugh. But both, he said, carried the same sense of responsibility.

“They weren’t trying to be heroes,” Andrew said. “They were just trying to take care of the people next to them.”

In their hometown, neighbors still remember the processions that brought the brothers home. Streets lined with flags. Fire trucks stationed along the route. Veterans standing at attention as the hearses passed.

At the family’s church, two small plaques now bear the Whitaker brothers’ names. Each Memorial Day, Robert and Elaine sit in the same pew while their sons are honored among the fallen.

Robert says he is proud of his boys. But pride, he has learned, does not soften grief.

“People want you to say it was worth it,” he said. “I can’t measure my sons’ lives that way. They were worth everything before they ever put on a uniform.”

The family still gathers for Sunday dinners, though two chairs are no longer filled. Elaine sets flowers near the photographs on birthdays. Andrew sometimes visits his brothers’ graves alone, telling them about ordinary things — work, weather, a game on television — because, he said, ordinary life is what he misses sharing with them most.

“There are days I’m angry. There are days I’m proud. Most days, I’m both,” Andrew said. “But I don’t want people to remember them only for how they died. I want them to remember that they lived.”

For Robert, that memory is now the family’s mission.

“They were our sons,” he said. “They were brothers. They were boys who loved home, who laughed at the dinner table, who called their mother just to check in. The war took them from us, but it doesn’t get to be the only thing that defines them.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
